Pregnancy

Cancer during pregnancy: diagnosis, treatment and infant feeding

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A cancer diagnosis during pregnancy can bring decisions you never expected to face alongside preparing for a baby. It is also possible to discover a pregnancy while already receiving cancer treatment. The next step is a coordinated discussion with the cancer and maternity teams: what the diagnosis means, which treatments are needed, and what can be offered at this stage of pregnancy. There is no single plan that applies to every cancer.

How often cancer occurs during pregnancy

Cancer is uncommon during pregnancy. SMFM estimates that a cancer diagnosis complicates approximately one in 1,000 pregnancies. NCI gives an approximate figure of one breast-cancer diagnosis per 3,000 pregnant women. These are population estimates, not predictions of an individual person’s risk, and figures vary with the population and period studied.

Cancer in people of reproductive age has become an increasing concern. Later childbearing is one relevant factor because the likelihood of many cancers rises with age, but it should not be treated as the only explanation or a reason to blame someone for the timing of a pregnancy.

Pregnancy does not mean that every cancer will grow faster. Its effects and the practical challenges of treatment vary by disease. In particular, a changing mole should be examined rather than attributed to pregnancy hormones; the American Academy of Dermatology does not identify pregnancy itself as an apparent increase in melanoma risk.

Which cancers can occur

Cancers diagnosed during pregnancy include breast, cervical, thyroid, ovarian and colorectal cancers, melanoma of the skin, leukemia, and Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma. These names describe different diseases with different treatments; a successful approach for one cannot simply be transferred to another.

Lung, brain and bone cancers can also occur, although they are less commonly encountered in pregnancy. The organ where a cancer began, its cell type and whether it has spread help determine the next steps. A list of possible cancers is not a screening checklist or a reason to assume that an everyday pregnancy symptom means cancer.

Symptoms still deserve investigation

Some warning signs overlap with changes that are common in pregnancy: tiredness, bloating, nausea, vomiting, headaches and breast changes. Rectal bleeding may come from hemorrhoids, but it should not automatically be dismissed as harmless. A new breast lump or a persistent change that is unusual for you needs assessment.

Tell your maternity clinician about symptoms that persist, worsen or return, including where they occur and how long they have lasted. Ask when to come back if an initial explanation or treatment does not resolve the problem. Pregnancy can make certain examinations harder to interpret, so follow-up matters.

These symptoms have many causes other than cancer. The purpose of reporting them is to find the cause, not to diagnose yourself from a list. If a symptom is severe or you feel acutely unwell, seek prompt medical assessment rather than waiting for the next routine appointment.

Pregnancy-related trophoblastic disease

Gestational trophoblastic disease, or GTD, is a separate group of uncommon conditions arising from cells associated with pregnancy. Trophoblast cells normally help form the placenta. In GTD, abnormal growth develops from this tissue; it is not simply an ordinary cancer that happens to coexist with pregnancy.

The group includes molar pregnancies and malignant conditions such as gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. Most GTD is not cancer, but some forms can invade or spread and need specialist treatment. Diagnosis, treatment and follow-up depend on the exact condition, so reassurance that a growth is “pregnancy related” should not replace the recommended monitoring.

Choosing imaging tests during pregnancy

A useful test answers a specific question: is there a mass, what tissue is involved, or has a confirmed cancer spread? Ultrasound uses sound waves, and MRI uses magnetic fields and radio waves rather than ionizing radiation. Ultrasound and MRI without contrast are often the first choices when they can provide the information needed.

X-rays and CT use ionizing radiation. The exposure reaching the fetus depends on the body area examined, the technique and the stage of pregnancy. Imaging the head or chest usually involves much less fetal exposure than directly imaging the abdomen or pelvis. This does not make every head scan automatically necessary or every abdominal scan automatically forbidden.

If a CT scan or another examination is clinically important, pregnancy alone should not prevent it. Tell the radiology team about the pregnancy and ask why the test is recommended and whether a suitable alternative would answer the same question. Contrast agents need their own benefit–risk assessment; an MRI with contrast is not the same decision as an MRI without it.

A lead apron is not the measure of whether a diagnostic examination has been planned safely. Current radiology guidance generally advises against routine fetal shielding during diagnostic X-ray imaging because it can obscure useful anatomy or interfere with the examination. Local policies vary. This advice concerns diagnostic imaging, not the planning of radiation treatment for cancer.

Biopsy, screening and a confirmed diagnosis

A biopsy removes cells or a small tissue sample for examination in a laboratory. Many biopsies can be performed during pregnancy, often with local anesthesia. The approach depends on the site, bleeding risk and whether a larger procedure or general anesthesia is needed. Tell the team and the pathologist that you are pregnant.

An examination and blood or urine tests may add important information, but an abnormal result is not necessarily a cancer diagnosis. For example, cervical screening can identify changes that need investigation; it does not by itself establish every case of cervical cancer. Similarly, an ultrasound may identify an ovarian mass without proving that the mass is malignant.

Ask which results confirm the diagnosis and which are being used to establish its extent, called staging. Knowing the cancer type and stage helps the team explain treatment choices more precisely than the word “cancer” alone.

Making a plan with the specialist team

Care normally involves an oncologist and specialist maternity care, with surgeons, radiologists, anesthetists, pharmacists and newborn specialists as needed. An oncologist is a doctor who treats cancer. More appointments than in an uncomplicated pregnancy may be needed, but you should still know who is coordinating the overall plan.

Decisions take account of the cancer’s type, location, size or spread, how quickly treatment is needed, your general health, the week of pregnancy and your priorities. Ask what is known about each option, what remains uncertain and what difference a delay would make in your own case.

A diagnosis does not automatically mean that a pregnancy must end. Many people can receive appropriate treatment while continuing pregnancy. Some aggressive cancers or urgently needed treatments create a serious conflict with continuing the pregnancy, and the team should explain the available options clearly. You deserve time and support appropriate to the urgency, without pressure or promises that any choice is risk free.

Surgery during pregnancy

Surgery may remove a tumor, obtain a diagnosis or form part of a wider treatment plan. The operation depends on the cancer and its location. Necessary cancer surgery should not be withheld simply because of pregnancy, including in the first trimester; the surgical and maternity teams plan anesthesia, monitoring and recovery together.

The phrase “surgery is possible” is different from saying that every operation has identical risks. Ask about the reason for the procedure, its expected benefit, the implications of waiting and how the pregnancy will be monitored.

Breast surgery may also affect feeding after birth. Removal of a breast prevents milk feeding from that breast, while the effect of other procedures depends on the tissue involved. Discuss feeding goals early, while recognizing that the treatment needed to control the cancer remains central to the plan.

Chemotherapy and other cancer medicines

Chemotherapy uses medicines that interfere with cancer cells. Some also affect rapidly developing fetal tissues. Exposure early in pregnancy can be particularly concerning because organs are forming, so treatment options in the first trimester are more restricted.

Selected chemotherapy regimens may be used later in pregnancy. The exact drugs, timing and reason for treatment matter; passing a particular pregnancy week does not make all chemotherapy safe. Ask what is known about the proposed regimen, including possible effects on fetal growth, early birth and longer-term follow-up.

Hormonal treatment, targeted medicines and immunotherapy are separate categories, with their own pregnancy restrictions and gaps in evidence. They cannot be assumed suitable because a chemotherapy regimen is sometimes used during pregnancy. For example, many breast-cancer hormonal and targeted treatments are postponed until after birth.

If you learn you are pregnant while receiving treatment, contact the oncology team promptly with the drug names and dates of treatment. Decisions need an individual exposure assessment. Do not replace that discussion with an online safety label or independently redesign the treatment schedule.

Radiotherapy needs a separate assessment

Radiotherapy treats cancer using high-energy radiation. Its doses and purpose are different from those of a diagnostic X-ray. Whether radiation could reach the fetus depends on the treatment field, dose, technique and pregnancy stage.

Radiotherapy is often deferred until after birth when that is an acceptable cancer-treatment plan. Treatment to the abdomen or pelvis is especially concerning, while exceptional treatment at a site farther away requires specialist planning. Later pregnancy is not a blanket safe period for radiotherapy. Ask the radiation oncologist what alternatives exist and what fetal exposure the proposed plan would involve.

Effects on the baby and placenta

Cancer in a pregnant person does not usually mean that the fetus has cancer. Direct spread across the placenta is extremely rare; melanoma is a recognized example. That is different from effects on the pregnancy caused by the illness, treatment, fetal growth changes or premature birth.

The maternity team may arrange extra growth scans and other monitoring according to the diagnosis and treatment. After birth, the baby’s assessment should take account of treatment exposure as well as the cancer itself. Current SMFM guidance recommends sending the placenta for pathological examination after cancer during pregnancy.

A baby who appears well at birth may still have a planned follow-up appointment. Ask who will review placental findings and whether the child needs any particular monitoring. A normal initial examination should not be used to cancel follow-up without the team’s advice.

Treatment timing and the birth plan

Sometimes a treatment can wait until later in pregnancy or after delivery; sometimes delay would compromise cancer care. An early-stage label alone does not establish that waiting is appropriate. The team should explain the expected trade-off for the specific disease rather than automatically postponing treatment until the last trimester.

An early birth is also not an automatic solution. Prematurity has its own consequences, so birth close to term is preferred when the medical situation allows. The choice of vaginal birth or cesarean depends on obstetric circumstances and any relevant effect of the cancer or its treatment.

Chemotherapy and birth usually need to be spaced to allow blood counts to recover and reduce infection or bleeding problems. The interval depends on the regimen and birth plan. Before leaving an appointment, ask what happens if labor starts earlier than expected and which team to contact.

Breastfeeding and expressed milk

Cancer is not transmitted to a baby through ordinary breastfeeding. However, that does not settle whether feeding is suitable during treatment. Medicines may enter breast milk, and surgery or radiation involving the breast can affect milk production. Some people treated for cancer can breastfeed, while others need a different feeding plan.

Breastfeeding is generally not recommended during cytotoxic chemotherapy. Many hormonal and targeted treatments also require avoiding breastfeeding. Milk expressed during an unsafe treatment interval does not become suitable for feeding merely because it has been refrigerated or frozen.

Whether breastfeeding can begin or resume depends on the exact medicine, the time since its last dose and any continuing treatment. There is no universal waiting period that fits all cancer drugs. Ask the oncology pharmacist and infant-feeding team for written instructions covering each treatment and any planned restart.

If breastfeeding is unavailable, insufficient or not what you want, ask for practical help choosing and using an appropriate alternative. Support with expressing, supply management or stopping milk production should be tailored to your wishes and treatment. Feeding decisions should not become another source of blame during cancer care.

Outlook and support after diagnosis

The outlook depends mainly on the particular cancer, its extent and whether effective treatment can be given. Pregnancy does not by itself establish a poor prognosis, and many people recover and have healthy children. Equally, a general reassurance that outcomes are always the same as outside pregnancy is too broad.

Delays in recognizing symptoms or starting necessary treatment can matter. Ask the team to distinguish what is known about your cancer from what is uncertain about pregnancy-specific evidence. A second specialist opinion can help with complex choices when it can be arranged without an unsafe delay.

Plan support for appointments, meals, childcare, rest and emotional wellbeing. A partner or trusted person can take notes if you want them involved, and the team can help arrange counseling or an interpreter. Cancer care continues after delivery; a clear handover and named contacts can make those first weeks more manageable.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Different cancers require different pregnancy and treatment plans.

Necessary investigation should not be delayed automatically because of pregnancy.

Fetal treatment exposure, cancer transmission and premature birth are different issues.

Milk safety requires advice about the exact treatment, not simply the cancer diagnosis.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to organize appointment questions and the agreed plan for tests, treatment, birth and feeding. Your oncology and maternity teams need to make the clinical decisions together.

When to seek help

Contact your cancer team promptly if you discover a pregnancy during treatment or develop a new concerning symptom. Follow the urgent-contact instructions from your treating team; do not change anticancer treatment from general online advice.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A pregnancy can often continue during appropriate cancer care, but decisions are individual.
  • A suspicious change still needs assessment even when it resembles a pregnancy symptom.
  • Surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and other medicines have different considerations.
  • Plan newborn follow-up and feeding before delivery where possible.
  • Ask for a coordinated plan and practical support for life after birth.

Frequently asked questions

How common is cancer during pregnancy?

SMFM estimates approximately one diagnosis per 1,000 pregnancies. This is a population estimate, not an individual prediction.

Does pregnancy automatically make cancer grow faster?

No. Cancer type and biology matter, and pregnancy can complicate detection and treatment. A changing mole, lump or persistent symptom still needs assessment.

Will an ultrasound or cervical screening test prove that I have cancer?

Not usually on its own. These tests may identify an abnormality needing further investigation. Diagnosis often requires a biopsy and specialist interpretation.

Should I refuse a CT scan while pregnant?

Discuss why it is needed with the radiology and maternity teams. A clinically important examination should not be rejected automatically; the scan and any contrast are planned for the situation.

Does diagnosis always mean ending the pregnancy?

No. Many people can continue pregnancy with appropriate treatment. Urgent or incompatible treatment can create difficult choices that require an individual specialist discussion.

Is every chemotherapy drug safe after the first trimester?

No. Only selected regimens are used, and their timing, fetal effects and follow-up need review. Other cancer-drug categories cannot be assumed to have the same safety profile.

Can cancer pass to my baby?

Direct transfer across the placenta is extremely rare. The care team considers the particular cancer, placental findings, treatment exposure and newborn follow-up rather than assuming either transmission or zero risk.

Will I need an early birth or a cesarean?

Not automatically. The birth plan depends on obstetric needs, cancer care and treatment timing. Avoiding unnecessary prematurity is an important part of planning.

Can I breastfeed during cancer treatment?

It depends on the treatment. Cytotoxic chemotherapy generally requires avoiding breastfeeding, and many other drugs do too. Ask for a medicine-specific plan for expressed milk and any later restart.

What should I do if I discover a pregnancy during treatment?

Contact your oncology team promptly with your treatment dates and medicines. They can coordinate an exposure assessment and maternity care rather than leaving you to make treatment decisions alone.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
